questions.stemHtml: While helping compile the team’s expense report, you notice that a well-liked colleague has been adding small, false amounts to his travel reimbursement claims for several months. What is the most appropriate action?

options.textHtml: Ignore it, since the amounts are small and raising it would hurt team morale.
Start adding similar small amounts to your own claims, since it is evidently tolerated.
Report the facts through the company’s prescribed channel (such as your manager, finance or the ethics helpline), without exaggeration or gossip.
Post about it in the office group chat so that everyone knows what he has been doing.

questions.solutionHtml:
Principle: honesty and proper process. False claims are a misuse of company money regardless of size; the right response is to report verifiable facts to the people responsible for handling them, which protects the organisation while keeping the matter fair to the colleague.

A condones fraud — small, repeated amounts are still dishonest. B makes you a participant. D humiliates the colleague publicly before any inquiry and bypasses due process.

questions.stemHtml: You are on a panel evaluating bids for a large contract. One bidder sends an expensive smartwatch to your home “as a festival gift”. What should you do?

options.textHtml: Politely return the gift and disclose the offer to your organisation as its policy requires.
Keep the gift but make sure it does not influence your evaluation.
Keep the gift and give the bidder slightly higher marks to return the courtesy.
Return the gift and quietly disqualify the bidder without telling anyone.

questions.solutionHtml:
Principle: avoid conflicts of interest and maintain transparency. A valuable gift from a bidder during an evaluation creates at least the appearance of bribery. Returning it and disclosing the offer protects both the process and you.

B still creates a conflict of interest — private intentions cannot be verified by others. C is accepting a bribe. D is a unilateral, undisclosed penalty; the decision on the bidder belongs to the process, not to you alone.

questions.stemHtml: Your manager has praised a report you submitted and forwarded it to senior leadership. You now discover a calculation error in it that changes one of its key recommendations. What is the best course of action?

options.textHtml: Say nothing, since the report has already been praised and the error may never be noticed.
Wait to see whether anyone notices, and correct it only if asked.
Quietly change the figures in your copy of the file without informing anyone.
Inform your manager promptly, explain the error and its impact, and provide a corrected version.

questions.solutionHtml:
Principle: accountability — own your mistakes, especially when others will act on them. Leadership may make decisions based on a wrong recommendation; prompt disclosure with a correction limits the harm.

A and B put your reputation ahead of the organisation’s decisions. C fixes nothing for the people already holding the wrong version and hides the error.

questions.stemHtml: In a leadership meeting, your team lead presents an idea you developed as if it were entirely his own. What is the most appropriate response?

options.textHtml: Interrupt the meeting and accuse him of stealing your idea in front of the leadership.
Later, speak to him privately and calmly about it, and keep a record of your contributions; escalate through proper channels only if the pattern continues.
Withhold your ideas from the team in future so that nobody can take credit for them.
Complain about him to colleagues so that his reputation suffers.

questions.solutionHtml:
Principle: a proportionate, respectful response that seeks to correct the wrong. A private conversation gives the lead a chance to set the record straight (it may have been careless rather than deliberate), and documentation plus formal escalation remain available if needed.

A is disproportionate and damages working relationships before he has had a chance to respond. C harms the team and the organisation, not just the lead. D is gossip — it damages reputations without resolving anything.

questions.stemHtml: You are asked to evaluate vendors for your company, and you find that one of the bidders is a firm owned by your cousin. You are confident you can be objective. What should you do?

options.textHtml: Disclose the relationship to your manager and step aside from evaluating that bid.
Evaluate all bids as usual, since you are confident you will be fair.
Reject your cousin’s bid outright to avoid any suspicion.
Tell your cousin the other bidders’ prices so the competition is “fair”.

questions.solutionHtml:
Principle: disclose and recuse when a personal interest could affect a decision. Fairness must be seen, not merely felt; other bidders and the employer cannot verify your inner objectivity.

B hides a real conflict of interest. C is unfair to your cousin’s firm, which may have the best bid — conflicts are handled by stepping aside, not by penalising the other party. D leaks confidential information and is clearly unethical.

questions.stemHtml: A quality engineer tells you that a batch of electric heaters ready for dispatch may have a wiring fault that could cause overheating. The sales team insists the batch must ship today to meet the quarterly target. As the plant manager, what should you do?

options.textHtml: Ship the batch and plan to recall it later if complaints arrive.
Ship the batch but add a small warning label asking customers to be careful.
Hold the batch, get the possible fault tested, and inform senior management of the delay and the reason.
Let the sales head decide, since targets are his responsibility.

questions.solutionHtml:
Principle: customer safety outweighs short-term financial targets. A plausible risk of fire must be checked before the product reaches customers; transparently informing management handles the business impact responsibly.

A knowingly exposes customers to harm. B shifts risk onto customers who cannot fix a wiring fault. D abdicates the plant manager’s responsibility for product safety.

questions.stemHtml: You work in a bank’s customer service team. A friend who has just started an insurance agency asks you for a list of customers’ phone numbers to call with offers. What should you do?

options.textHtml: Share only the phone numbers, not account details, since that is harmless.
Share the list only with customers who have high balances.
Ask your friend to pay for the list.
Refuse, explaining that customer data is confidential and cannot be shared without proper authorisation and consent.

questions.solutionHtml:
Principle: confidentiality and respect for customer consent. Customers gave their data to the bank for banking purposes; passing it to a third party for marketing breaches their trust and the bank’s rules.

A and B are still unauthorised disclosure — phone numbers are personal data. C adds selling confidential information to the breach.

questions.stemHtml: Your manager privately tells you to reject all job applicants from a particular community, regardless of their qualifications. What should you do?

options.textHtml: Follow the instruction, since the manager is responsible for hiring decisions.
Decline to follow the instruction, continue to assess candidates on merit, and report the instruction to HR or the appropriate authority.
Follow the instruction but keep a note of it in case of future trouble.
Resign immediately without informing anyone of the reason.

questions.solutionHtml:
Principle: fairness and equal opportunity — candidates must be judged on merit. Discriminating by community is unjust and typically unlawful; an instruction from a superior does not make it acceptable. Reporting it allows the organisation to stop it.

A and C make you a participant in discrimination. D avoids personal involvement but leaves the injustice in place for every future applicant.

options.textHtml: Acting consistently with one’s ethical principles, even when no one is watching and it is personally costly.
Following every instruction given by a superior without question.
Being popular and well liked by one’s colleagues.
Achieving one’s targets by whatever means are available.

questions.solutionHtml:
A is correct. Integrity means a consistent match between one’s values and one’s actions, independent of observation or reward.

B describes obedience, which can conflict with integrity when instructions are wrong. C is popularity. D describes an ends-justify-the-means approach, which is the opposite of integrity.

questions.stemHtml: On your way to college, you find a wallet on the road containing ₹8,000 in cash and the owner’s identity card with an address. What is the most appropriate action?

options.textHtml: Keep the cash and post the empty wallet to the owner.
Keep the wallet, since the owner was careless and you found it fairly.
Return the wallet with all its contents to the owner, or hand it in at the nearest police station.
Donate the cash to charity and throw away the wallet.

questions.solutionHtml:
Principle: honesty and respect for others’ property. Finding something does not make it yours; the owner can be identified, so everything should go back to them (directly or via the police).

A and B are taking someone else’s money. D may sound generous, but it is giving away money that is not yours to give.
